opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, my first reaction was that it makes a lot of sense, though I should say I'm interpreting from the outside. I don't know the internal details of the decision.

Andrej has always been someone who likes to understand things from first principles. He wants to build the whole stack himself and see where the gradients flow. Pre-training is still where much of the fundamental capability of these models comes from. People talk a lot about post-training, RL, and agents, and those matter enormously, but the base model sets the ceiling. So for someone like him, going back to pre-training is going back to the core of the problem.

The "auto research" part is, to me, the more interesting signal. Over the past year or two, many of us have been asking whether these models can do research themselves: propose hypotheses, write the experiment code, run it, read the results, and iterate. If that loop starts to work even partially, the pace of progress changes. You're no longer bottlenecked by how many good researchers you can hire. You're bottlenecked by compute and by how well you can verify what the model produces. Anthropic has clearly been thinking seriously about this, and pairing it with pre-training is natural. The research you most want to automate is research on making the next model better.

There's also a broader trend. The top labs are converging on the view that the frontier isn't just one bigger model. It's a system that improves itself, with humans moving up a level to setting directions, judging taste, and catching mistakes. That's where people with deep intuition, like Andrej, become even more valuable, not less. Someone has to know which of the hundred experiments the model ran actually matters.

My one caveat, from my own experience doing research, is that the hardest part isn't running experiments. It's knowing which question is worth asking and recognizing when a surprising result is real rather than a bug. That's still very hard to automate. So I'd watch whether this effort produces genuinely new ideas or mostly speeds up the search within ideas humans already have. Either outcome would be useful, but they're quite different.

r001.rationale: The candidate frames auto research as part of a broader trend, saying top labs are converging on systems that improve themselves and that Anthropic is taking model-led research seriously.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's a pretty telling signal, actually, on a couple of levels.

First, on the person. Andrej has always gravitated toward whatever he thinks is the most fundamental, most "leverage" problem at a given moment. At OpenAI early on it was the core research, at Tesla it was turning vision into a real production system, then he spent a stretch basically teaching the whole world how these models work from scratch. He doesn't chase titles. So when someone like that picks pre-training plus "auto research," he's telling you where he thinks the frontier actually is.

Second, on pre-training specifically. There's been this narrative for a year or two that pre-training is "done," that all the action moved to post-training, RL, reasoning, agents. I never fully bought that, and I think this move says the people closest to the problem don't either. The base model is still the ceiling for everything downstream. Data quality, curriculum, how you spend compute, how you make scaling more efficient instead of just bigger, these are still wide open. A lot of what looks like a post-training breakthrough is really the base model finally having the right representation underneath.

Third, and this is the part I find most interesting, the "auto research" piece. That's the idea of using the models themselves to run the research loop: propose hypotheses, write the experiments, read the results, iterate. If you believe that works even partially, it changes the economics of a lab. You're no longer bottlenecked by how many strong researchers you can hire. You're bottlenecked by compute and by how good your model is at doing science. And notice how that connects back to pre-training: a better base model is a better researcher, and a better researcher improves the base model. That's the flywheel every lab wants, and it's a very natural thing for Andrej to want to be in the middle of, because he's always cared about the end-to-end system, not just one component.

As for why Anthropic rather than somewhere else, I'd be careful not to over-read it, but Anthropic has been very clear about betting on exactly this recursive, model-accelerates-research direction, and they have a culture that tolerates long, somewhat unglamorous infrastructure work. Pre-training is unglamorous. The payoff is delayed. You need an organization that is patient about that.

So my read: it's not a pivot away from the "agents era," it's a bet that the agents era is going to be won by whoever builds the best foundation and the fastest research loop on top of it. And it's a reminder to all of us that the fundamentals aren't solved just because the discourse moved on.

r001.rationale: The response frames “auto research” as models running and improving the research loop, calls the resulting flywheel something every lab wants, and presents Karpathy’s move as a bet on that direction.

astra-6.text:
If that’s accurate, I’d read it as a bet on two things: that pre-training still has substantial room to improve, and that AI can help us discover those improvements faster. I wouldn’t infer his personal motivations without hearing from him directly.

Pre-training and automated research are closely connected. When you train a model, you’re making decisions about data, architectures, objectives, and optimization. There are far more experiments you could run than you have time or compute for. An AI research assistant could help formulate hypotheses, implement experiments, analyze results, and decide what to try next.

The difficult part is closing that loop reliably. Writing training code is one step; recognizing whether an improvement is real, understanding why it happened, and deciding whether it will survive at a larger scale are much harder. You can easily automate a lot of experiments that don’t teach you anything.

So the interesting question for me is whether AI can increase the amount of useful research we get per unit of compute. Better models could help us do better research, and better research could produce better models. That feedback loop is a compelling direction, but making it work requires much more than having an agent run experiments unattended.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes AI-assisted research and a feedback loop between better models and better research, but it does not say this indicates self-improvement or self-learning is becoming a mainstream research direction.

sol-6.1.text:
If that’s the move he’s making, I’d interpret it as a bet on two connected ideas: that pre-training still has substantial room to improve, and that AI can help us discover those improvements faster.

Pre-training research involves a lot of experimentation. You have an idea, implement it, run an experiment, inspect the results, and decide what to try next. The interesting question with automated research is how much of that loop a model can handle. Can it just write the code, or can it propose a useful hypothesis, recognize that an experiment is misleading, and change direction?

That distinction matters. Running more experiments is valuable, but choosing the right experiments is much harder. If AI gets better at that, you could have a feedback loop where stronger models help produce the next generation of stronger models.

So I’d see the combination of pre-training and automated research as particularly interesting. But I wouldn’t infer someone’s exact motivation from a job move alone.

r001.rationale: The response interprets the move as a bet on improving pre-training through automated research, including a feedback loop where models help produce stronger models. It does not communicate that self-improvement or self-learning is becoming a mainstream research direction.
